items: One chain, three layers. Upstream supplies chips and core components, midstream turns parts into systems and buildings into powered data halls, and downstream operates capacity and trades compute — with end applications ultimately paying for the whole chain.

The binding constraints are power and electrical equipment. Gas turbines and transformers are structural shortages (OEMs either won't or can't add capacity); memory and advanced packaging are tight but expanding; cooling and optics are self-correcting. Downstream delays are transmitted, not home-grown.

Credit lives downstream and on the power side; upstream is equity territory. Two questions — what repays the loan, and what can be seized if it isn't repaid — place colo, hyperscaler SPVs, neoclouds, power generation and software ARR in credit bands, while fabless chips, optics, AI labs and apps remain equity stories.

Cost of capital is compressing fast. CoreWeave moved from private credit to high yield to an A3-rated GPU-backed facility within roughly two years (CoreWeave, May-24; CoreWeave 8-K, Sep-26; CoreWeave, Mar-26); the Meta-vs-Hyperion gap shows a ~150bp structural premium available to private credit on the same underlying credit (Junson calculation).
Under-appreciated angles. ODM inventory and receivables financing (ABF), power-side project finance, and sponsor direct lending behind PE roll-ups of electrical-equipment and cooling niche champions.

blocks.text: Value Chain
Three layers: from chips to the end-user

blocks.html: We map the data center value chain in three layers. Upstream supplies semiconductors and core components: the GPU die and HBM memory are packaged together into a single device through TSMC's CoWoS process; the packaged chip is then soldered onto a substrate/PCB (the chip's "seat"); optical modules are not part of the package at all but plug into switches to connect racks. Upstream also includes CPUs, networking and power semiconductors, and the equipment/materials layer behind the foundries; we focus on the five components above as they carry the bulk of AI server bill-of-materials value and are where supply bottlenecks and pricing power currently sit. Midstream turns components into complete systems and buildings into powered data halls — power equipment, building-level cooling, server assembly, networking, and design/EPC. Midstream turns components into complete systems and buildings into powered data halls — power equipment, building-level cooling, server assembly, networking, and design/EPC. Midstream itself splits into two production lines: one assembles components into complete racks, the other turns shells into powered halls. Behind both sits power generation — increasingly procured directly by data centers as electricity becomes the binding constraint: power is the new land. Downstream operates the capacity, trades compute, and ultimately sells to the end applications that pay for the entire chain.

blocks.html: Downstream has its own internal structure. Third-party colocation providers are the landlord layer, renting space to hyperscalers and neoclouds. Hyperscalers span two layers: they build their own data centers (acting as landlords), sell cloud compute externally, and are simultaneously the largest tenant of colo operators and the largest buyer of neocloud capacity. Neoclouds are the compute layer — effectively compute "sub-landlords" that lease halls, fill them with GPUs and rent out compute. AI model labs are the demand layer and the ultimate large buyers of compute. Software and data platforms form a horizontal service layer — managing data and orchestrating training for labs, running data backends and model calls for applications — riding total volume without taking single-name risk.

blocks.text: The AI value chain vs the data center value chain

blocks.html: The commonly cited AI value chain — ① compute & infrastructure, ② data, ③ models, ④ tooling/middleware, ⑤ applications — describes how intelligence is produced. It compresses the entire physical world (chips, servers, data centers, cloud) into a single foundation layer ①. The data center value chain describes how money and hardware flow, and is essentially an enlargement of that first layer, split into upstream, midstream and downstream operations. The remaining layers map one-to-one: labs (③) buy compute from the operating layer, applications (⑤) pay for the chain, and data (②) plus tooling (④) collapse into our horizontal software-and-data-platform layer, which sells tools to models, applications and enterprises but sits outside the main compute payment chain.

blocks.text: Supply Bottlenecks
Constraints sit upstream and midstream; downstream delays are transmitted

blocks.html: Supply bottlenecks are concentrated in the upstream and midstream layers; downstream bottlenecks are transmitted ones — colo and hyperscaler deliveries are held up by power and electrical equipment rather than by capital or demand. The binding constraint has migrated down the physical stack: GPUs in 2023, HBM and advanced packaging through 2024–25, and now power and electrical equipment — each successive bottleneck sitting on a longer replacement cycle than the last. We rank nine bottleneck points by how long we expect each to persist (Exhibit 4).

blocks.html: Power side is the deepest constraint. GE Vernova's gas turbine backlog plus slot reservations rose to 116GW in 2Q26, from 100GW in 1Q26, and the company now targets at least 125GW by year-end. Siemens Energy's turbine capacity is booked out to FY2028 with 2029–30 slots filling quickly, and group-wide lead times now run three years or more. On the grid side, large (>100MW) connections in Northern Virginia can take up to seven years. Electrical equipment is next: large power transformer lead times have stretched to as long as 4–5 years, with US prices up ~79% (FT), while data-center-class switchgear is quoted at 52–84+ weeks and medium-voltage gear is sold out through 2028 in many channels. Transformer capacity is further gated by grain-oriented electrical steel supply and a retiring winding workforce — constraints that cannot be hired or built quickly.

blocks.html: Critically, suppliers are choosing not to expand. Turbine and transformer makers were burned by the last capacity cycle and cannot verify how much of today's order book is double-ordering or speculative projects; their rational response is to stretch lead times, raise prices and demand multi-year reservations with deposits rather than build new plants — effectively repricing the risk onto buyers. This supply discipline is itself the most honest read on demand quality: equipment makers see who is double-ordering, and they are voting with their capex. A large greenfield expansion announcement from GE Vernova or Siemens Energy would be the clearest signal that suppliers finally believe the demand.

blocks.html: Inside the rack, the constraint has moved to what surrounds the GPU. AI data centers are expected to absorb ~70% of global memory output in 2026; SK hynix has sold out its entire 2026 production, and Gartner forecasts 2026 DRAM prices +125%. The shortage is structural rather than cyclical: HBM consumes roughly 4x the wafer capacity per bit of standard DRAM, so every HBM allocation crowds out conventional supply, and the three-player oligopoly — burned by past cycles — is deliberately underbuilding rather than chasing the spike. NVIDIA has booked more than half of TSMC's CoWoS capacity for 2026–27. Construction is stretched too: more than 66GW is under construction in North America (JLL), and ~40% of US data centers due in 2026 are at risk of delay. Agentic AI is pulling CPU:GPU ratios from 1:8 towards 1:1, with Intel describing unmet demand as "starting with a B" and server CPU prices up 10–20% since March. GPUs themselves are the least severe of the chip constraints — lead times of 36–52 weeks — supply is catching up, but scarcity pricing clearly persists at the rental layer: CoreWeave still raised prices ~25% across SKUs in July. Liquid cooling and optics/PCB are self-correcting bottlenecks with 6–12-month capacity expansion cycles.

blocks.text: Won't vs can't: why the two deepest shortages are structural

blocks.html: Gas turbines — manufacturers won't expand. The core reason is doubt over demand quality. Turbine OEMs (GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, Mitsubishi) remember the last cycle vividly: in the mid-2010s the industry went through a brutal overcapacity phase after betting on global gas-fired demand, only for renewables to scale and orders to collapse — both Siemens' and GE's power divisions went through layoffs and restructuring. Today data center demand has pushed order books to record highs, but OEMs know the book contains froth: the same project may solicit quotes from all three vendors at once (duplicate orders); many "planned" AI campuses will never secure funding or power (speculative projects); and if hyperscaler capex turns, orders could evaporate together. Spending billions on new factories for demand that may not materialise would, if demand is disproved around 2028, simply become the next write-down. The rational choice is therefore not to expand, but to stretch lead times, raise prices, and require customers to order 6–8 years ahead with heavy deposits (AID deck notes) — shifting risk to the buyer, which is both more profitable and safer than building capacity.

blocks.html: Transformers — manufacturers largely can't expand. The bottleneck sits in two physical inputs. The first is grain-oriented electrical steel (GOES), the core material for transformer cores, where global capacity is highly concentrated (the US has essentially one major domestic producer) and steel mills also need years to expand. The second is skilled labour for winding and assembly: large transformers remain substantially hand-built, winders take years to train, and this workforce in Europe and the US is entering a retirement wave — not being able to hire is more binding than not being able to build a factory. Testing adds a third constraint, as every large unit must pass high-voltage factory testing and test bays are themselves scarce capacity. Even where OEMs want to expand, ramp-up is measured in multi-year steps.

Equity or Credit? The Positioning Map
Two questions decide the instrument

blocks.html: Credit asks two core questions: ① what repays the loan? — the predictability of cash flow (x-axis); and ② what can the lender take if it isn't repaid? — collateral (y-axis). If at least one answer is good, the segment is credit-investable; if both are weak, it is an equity story, where returns depend on share price and exit rather than coupon. Equity, by contrast, is investable everywhere on the map — the axes gate credit, not equity. What shifts across the chart is the equity return profile: in the top-right, equity earns development spreads and rental distributions on hard, contracted assets (infrastructure-style); in the bottom-left, it earns pure growth and multiple expansion (venture-style). The map therefore answers two different questions at once: where credit can play, and what kind of equity you are buying. Two credit bands emerge: an asset-backed band (ABS, project bonds, ABF — secured on assets, with rental or amortising coupons) in the top-right, and a cash-flow band (direct lending against ARR — secured on cash flow, with floating coupons that can deliver 8%+ cash yield) in the bottom-right.

blocks.html: The test is how long and how hard the contracts that lock in revenue are, and whether customers can walk away at will. Far right (0.8–0.9): colo (10–15-year leases, mostly investment-grade tenants (industry convention) — the rightmost point); hyperscaler SPVs (Hyperion's lease payments are locked in directly by Meta's contract (IFR; WSJ / Bloomberg, Oct-25)); power-side generation (PPAs typically 10–20 years (industry convention)); and software ARR (annual or multi-year subscriptions with NRR persistently above 100% (industry convention) — customers cannot easily leave). Mid-high (~0.7): neoclouds hold multi-year take-or-pay contracts (CoreWeave's backlog is the evidence), but these are shorter than colo leases and counterparties are highly concentrated, so they sit left of colo. Middle (0.4–0.6): foundry and packaging (capacity reservations and prepayments are semi-contractual, but the business is still order-driven); EPC (contracted during a project, but a new job must be won when it ends); server ODMs (frame agreements, but in practice PO-driven); and power equipment (multi-year backlogs look locked in, but they are one-off equipment sales, not recurring revenue). Far left (0.1–0.3): optics and memory (quarterly-negotiated commodity pricing that booms and busts with the cycle — the recent ~60% memory price jump (AID deck notes) precisely shows there is no contractual protection); GPU designers (cancellable orders, cyclical demand); AI labs (subscriptions and API usage are growing, but customers can switch at any time); and end applications (monthly subscriptions, very high churn).

blocks.html: The test is whether there is something that can be taken, sold and still hold value after default, and whether it can be ring-fenced in an SPV and financed on its own. Very high (0.8+): power-side generation (power plants are textbook collateral: long-lived, with cash flows tied to the asset and single-project financeable); colo (building + land + power-interconnection rights, and halls can be re-let to new tenants, so resale is good); foundry and packaging (fabs are the heaviest fixed assets in the chain — with an honest caveat that fabs are highly specialised and actually resell poorly, so their "hardness" is more about capital intensity and replacement value). Mid-high (0.6–0.75): hyperscaler SPVs (data centers are hard assets, but build-to-suit single-tenant facilities are harder to re-let than colo, so they sit slightly below colo); neoclouds (GPUs are genuinely seizable and resaleable — the premise of GPU financing — but lose half their value within two to three years; the steep residual curve keeps them mid-chart, and that gap is exactly why Lambda-style pure-residual loans are risky). Middle (0.3–0.55): memory (owns fabs and is asset-heavy — higher than fabless GPU designers); power equipment, EPC, liquid cooling and ODMs (they own plants and lines, but these are general-purpose manufacturing assets; ODMs are a special case, as their truly financeable "assets" are inventory and receivables — short-duration and monetisable, which is where the ABF angle comes from, but not long-lived hard assets). Very low (0.1–0.35): GPU/ASIC designers (fabless — NVIDIA's assets are IP and design teams, not factories); optics (asset-light manufacturing); AI labs (assets are model weights and people, neither of which can be taken); software and end applications (code is not collateral).

blocks.text: Row-by-row read

items: ① Upstream chips (GPU / memory / foundry). Public equity is deep — among the largest-cap, most liquid sectors globally. PE is "some": semiconductor buyout funds and custom-chip pre-IPO rounds exist, but targets are scarce and often subject to foreign-investment review, so this is not a pipeline. IG is deep: NVIDIA, TSMC and Micron are active, large IG issuers. ABS is structurally absent — fabless has no assets to put in an SPV, and fab owners such as TSMC have no need for off-balance-sheet funding. DL/ABF is absent because cash cows don't borrow expensive private money. Infra equity is absent: a fab is not an infrastructure asset (it cannot be re-let).

② Optics / PCB / substrate. Public equity is deep, with ample A-share and Taiwan liquidity. PE is "some" (occasional M&A); IG/HY is "some" (leaders issue, but in limited size). DL/ABF is "some": supply-chain finance and receivables factoring exist, but tickets are small and fragmented — a niche, not a main battlefield. ABS is absent for lack of long-term contracted cash flows.

③ Power equipment / cooling. Public equity is deep — Eaton and Vertiv have been among the best-performing industrials of the AI cycle. This is the only deep PE cell in the midstream: transformer, switchgear and liquid-cooling niche champions are an active PE hunting ground, KKR–CoolIT is the marquee deal (KKR, 2023), and the roll-up logic is repeatable (that repeatability is what separates "deep" here from "some" in the row above). IG is "some" — industrial majors issue, but it is not an incremental story. DL/ABF is "some": sponsor acquisition finance follows PE deals and order surges create ABL demand, so the pipeline is real but dependent on PE activity. ABS and infra equity are absent (no contracted cash flow; not infrastructure assets).

④ Server ODM. Public equity is deep (heavyweight Taiwan ODMs); IG is "some" (e.g. Hon Hai). DL/ABF is "some": inventory financing and factoring to pre-fund GPU inventory are real and growing, but rated "some" rather than "deep" because banks and supply-chain finance still carry most of it and specialist-fund penetration is shallow — we see this as one of the cells most likely to deepen. PE is absent: the manufacturers are too large and family- or group-controlled, with no M&A entry point.

⑤ Design & EPC. The shallowest row in the table. Public equity is absent — mostly private firms or sub-units of construction groups, with no pure plays. PE is "some" (occasional contractor M&A). DL/ABF is "some" but weak: project bridge loans and subcontractor factoring exist but are extremely fragmented and regional. Everything else is absent — no assets, no long contracts, no bond issuance. The investment implication is to reach EPC through other rows: its cycle shows up in midstream equipment order books and downstream development-loan demand.

⑥ Power-side generation. The only row with deep cells in both infra equity and ABS/project bonds. Infra equity is deep — dedicated and behind-the-meter power plants are classic infrastructure-fund assets with ample pipeline; project finance is a century-old mature market in the power sector. Public equity is "some" (IPPs such as Vistra and Constellation are investable, but few). PE and IG are "some" — present but not the main channel. DL/ABF is "some" through infra debt funds doing mezzanine and HoldCo. This row is essentially the standard portrait of infrastructure as an asset class.

⑦ Colo. The only row with four deep cells in a row, each backed by hard evidence: public equity (Equinix and Digital Realty, two large-cap REITs); infra equity (Vantage, Aligned and STACK are all fund-owned platforms — a repeatable strategy); IG (Equinix and Digital Realty are active issuers); and ABS (data center securitisation reached $27bn in 2025 (KBRA, Mar-26), with Vantage alone at ~$7.5bn across nine deals (CNBC; TechRepublic, Jun-25)). PE is marked absent not because there is no private equity, but because private equity in these assets is infra equity — the two columns are not double-counted. DL/ABF is "some": private debt funds provide mezzanine and development loans, growing in volume but still secondary to ABS.

⑧ Hyperscaler. Public equity is deep. IG is deep — Meta's single $30bn deal drew a $125bn book (S&P via FI Desk, Oct-25), within ~$157bn of tech bond issuance in 2025 (AID deck notes). ABS/project bonds are deep, and this cell was shallow a year ago: the $27.3bn Hyperion deal (IFR; WSJ / Bloomberg, Oct-25) took the hyperscaler off-balance-sheet SPV from non-existent to the largest private credit transaction on record — the fastest colour change in the table. Infra equity is "some": Blue Owl's 80% stake in the JV (IFR; WSJ / Bloomberg, Oct-25) is infra equity exposure, but access is scarce and deal-by-deal. PE is absent (too large to buy) and DL/ABF is absent (AA-rated issuers don't need expensive private money).

⑨ Neocloud. Public equity is deep (CoreWeave and Nebius are listed). IG/HY/converts are deep: CoreWeave alone has five high-yield notes and three convertibles outstanding (CoreWeave 8-K, Sep-26), and Nebius has issued converts repeatedly (>$10bn cumulatively per the deck (AID deck notes)) — the public coupon market is established. DL/ABF is deep: GPU- and contract-secured lending is the sector's signature, from CoreWeave's successive DDTL facilities (CoreWeave, Mar-26) to Lambda's Macquarie facility (Lambda, Apr-24), and specialist AI-infrastructure credit funds have emerged. PE/growth is "some" (Crusoe and Lambda pre-IPO rounds, but the window is narrowing). ABS is "some": GPU securitisation and data center project debt exist as one-offs (e.g. Crusoe–JPMorgan (press reports, 2025)) but no Vantage-style issuance platform yet. Infra equity is absent — neoclouds mostly lease halls rather than own infrastructure.

⑩ AI labs. PE/growth is deep — mega private rounds plus secondaries are currently the only scaled way these companies raise money. IG/HY/converts is "some": only bank revolvers and sporadic arrangements (OpenAI's ~$4bn facility, undrawn (OpenAI, Oct-24)); the public bond market is not open. DL/ABF is "some" but weak: direct private lending to labs barely exists, and exposure has to route through compute vehicles (the xAI SPV (Bloomberg, Oct-25) is an exception and controversial). Everything else is absent — no assets (weights and people), not infrastructure, not listed. Note that Google/Meta lab exposure is classified under the hyperscaler row to avoid double counting.

⑪ Software & data platforms. Public equity is deep (the SaaS sector); PE is deep — software buyouts are one of PE's largest verticals. DL/ABF is deep: ARR lending is the business on which direct lending funds were built, with pipeline, funds and two decades of history (the CDLI's 10.4% asset-level income (Cliffwater, Mar-26) is largely this asset type). IG is "some" (large software issuers). ABS and infra equity are absent — this row is the textbook case of answering only the cash-flow question, so debt depth appears only in the cash-flow-secured column.

⑫ End applications. PE/growth is deep — VC home turf. Public equity is "some" (listed app companies exist, but few pure plays). DL/ABF is "some": venture debt exists but is small, and AI app retention has not been tested through a cycle, so it cannot support ARR-lending leverage. Everything else is absent — no assets, no long contracts, no bond issuance.

blocks.text: Upstream: Sub-sector Detail
Primer: fab, fabless, foundry and IDM

blocks.html: A fab (fabrication plant) is a wafer fab — the factory that turns silicon wafers into chips. A leading-edge fab costs tens of billions of dollars, its equipment is highly specialised and depreciation is heavy, which is what "asset-heavy" means in this report. Fabless companies have no fab: they only design chips and outsource manufacturing. NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom and Marvell design chips, have TSMC manufacture them and OSATs package them; their assets are mainly IP, design teams and software ecosystems — hence high gross margins and ROE, but almost no pledgeable hard assets on the balance sheet. Around the fab, semiconductor companies fall into three models: fabless (design only — NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom; asset-light, high margin); foundry (pure-play manufacturing for others, no own brand — TSMC, SMIC; asset-heavy); and IDM (integrated design and manufacturing — Micron, SK hynix, Samsung, Intel; also asset-heavy).

blocks.text: Four upstream conclusions

items: ① Equity territory; credit penetration ≈0. Fabless leaves nothing to seize in liquidation, and cash cows don't borrow expensive private money. The investable toolkit upstream is essentially public equity plus IG bonds; only packaging/OSAT equipment finance leases offer an ABF angle.

② The bottleneck has moved from the GPU to what surrounds it. Memory: data centers take ~70% of 2026 global output (IDC via The Motley Fool, Jun-26), SK hynix is sold out (SK hynix via Computing, 2026) and Gartner sees DRAM +125% (Gartner, Apr-26). Packaging: CoWoS is sold out with NVIDIA holding more than half of 2026–27 capacity (DigiTimes, Dec-25). The chokepoint is now the supporting components, not the GPU itself.

③ The packaging boundary is expanding (CPO). Today TSMC packages only GPU + HBM; co-packaged optics bring the optical engine into the switch-chip package. Optics is moving from a rack plug-in to an in-package component — the biggest long-term debate for the optics sector: displacement, or an upgrade to optical-engine supplier.

④ The reverse-financier signal. Chipmakers have started acting as financiers: NVIDIA committed up to $2bn to xAI's GPU financing SPV (Bloomberg, Oct-25) and $2bn each to Nebius (pre-funded warrants) and CoreWeave (Nebius 6-K / TheNextWeb, Mar-26). The "circular financing" debate is a live test of how real end-demand is.

blocks.text: Four midstream conclusions

items: ① Backlog ≠ recurring revenue. Equipment makers' backlogs are one-off sales; from a credit perspective, backlog should not be treated as contracted cash flow. From an equity perspective, power equipment has been one of the best-performing industrial groups of the AI cycle.

② The hardest bottleneck in the chain sits here. Transformer lead times of 4–5 years with US prices ~+79% (FT; BloombergNEF, 2026); Siemens Energy turbines booked out to FY2028 (S&P Global, Jun-26) and GE Vernova's backlog plus slots at 116GW (GE Vernova 2Q26 results, Jul-26) — and OEMs are reluctant to expand for fear demand won't materialise. The bottleneck is pricing power, and at the same time the source of downstream delay risk.

③ The under-appreciated ABF angle. ODMs pre-fund large GPU inventories and receivables before delivering racks → inventory financing and factoring. Meanwhile PE is buying niche champions (KKR–CoolIT (KKR, 2023)), with sponsor direct lending following behind.

④ Power-side is the mid/downstream interface. It is project finance territory and links naturally to downstream development loans — when assessing a colo development pipeline, the power-side order book is effectively its delivery schedule.

blocks.text: Four downstream conclusions

items: ① Credit's main battlefield. The only full-capital-structure row sits here (colo): development loans → ABS ($27bn issued in 2025 (KBRA, Mar-26)) → mezzanine → IG, every layer investable. Long leases plus hard assets answer both credit questions at once.

② Cost-of-capital compression is the main theme. The spread alpha earned by early private credit is being competed away by public markets.

③ Same borrower, two tracks: the structural premium. The ~150bp difference (Junson calculation) is the structural premium captured by private credit.

④ The bottleneck is transmitted. This layer lacks neither capital nor demand; delivery is held up by power and equipment, with 30–50% of US capacity planned for 2026 expected to be delayed or cancelled (Bloomberg citing Sightline Climate, May-26). blocks.text: Downside Risks
Five risks that cut across the chain

blocks.html: Before sub-sector specifics, five risks operate at the level of the whole chain — they are correlated with each other, and most sub-sector risks below are local expressions of them.
blocks.text: Before sub-sector specifics, five risks operate at the level of the whole chain — they are correlated with each other, and most sub-sector risks below are local expressions of them.

items: End-demand shortfall is the master risk. Capex has been deployed years ahead of the application revenue that must ultimately service it; the gap is bridged by leases and debt. If monetisation disappoints, stress travels up the payment chain in reverse order: application churn hits lab revenue, labs renegotiate or walk from compute commitments, neocloud backlog stops converting, colo re-leasing weakens, and equipment orders cancel last. The first casualties are the weakest counterparties' take-or-pay contracts and GPU residual values — precisely the two collateral types that anchor this cycle's credit structures.

The 2028 oversupply flip. Today's queues contain duplicate and speculative orders that suppliers cannot verify. Supply discipline delays capacity but does not eliminate it: expansions already sanctioned land in 2027–28, just as any double-ordering unwinds. Shortage can flip to glut across turbines, transformers and data hall capacity simultaneously — the pattern of the mid-2010s gas-turbine bust and the 2001 fibre glut, where order books looked strongest immediately before cancellation waves.

Circular financing unwind. NVIDIA capital inside customer SPVs, pre-funded warrants and equity stakes (Bloomberg, Oct-25; Nebius 6-K / TheNextWeb, Mar-26) means part of reported demand is supported by the supplier's own balance sheet. If vendor financing pulls back, marginal buyers lose funding and the true level of unsupported demand is discovered — with the markdown concentrated in exactly the GPU-backed paper that vendor support made financeable.

Rates, duration and the refinancing wall. The risk runs at both ends of the curve. Long-duration structures (Hyperion at 23.6 years (IFR; WSJ / Bloomberg, Oct-25)) carry mark-to-market duration risk even without credit deterioration. At the short end, neocloud debt matures years before the contracts and assets it funds; a 2027–28 maturity wall meeting wider spreads — which gap out precisely in risk-off — is the sector's classic failure mode.

Counterparty concentration. The chain's cash flows funnel through fewer than ten names — NVIDIA, four hyperscalers, a handful of labs. A single strategy change at any of them reprices entire sub-sectors, and because the same names sit on both the demand and supply side of many contracts, diversification across sub-sectors is partly illusory: one decision can hit a portfolio through several positions at once.

The classic memory cycle: the oligopoly adds capacity into a demand pause and prices halve within quarters — the +125% forecast can reverse as fast as it built; HBM qualification loss at a lead customer strands committed capacity.
All three IDMs announcing capex expansion together; contract prices rolling over; HBM share shifts at NVIDIA.

CoWoS overbuild meets demand digestion, cutting utilisation on highly specialised lines with poor resale value; single-customer concentration (NVIDIA >50% of allocation (DigiTimes, Dec-25)) makes utilisation hostage to one roadmap; Taiwan concentration is the standing geopolitical tail.
TSMC AI-related capex / revenue guidance; CoWoS pricing on renewal.
Low technical barriers mean capacity responds within 12 months and margins compress first among the five components; spec transitions (layer counts, materials) strand older lines.
Quote lead times normalising; ASP trend at leaders.

CPO is a terminal-value question: if optics move into the package, pluggable-module makers are displaced or demoted to component suppliers; meanwhile each generation brings ~annual price erosion, and demand is concentrated in a few hyperscalers.
CPO switch shipment ramp at Broadcom / NVIDIA; 1.6T ASP trajectory.
The agentic 1:1 CPU:GPU thesis may not materialise at scale — the CPU squeeze would then unwind quickly; x86 share loss to ARM-based server CPUs continues regardless of the AI cycle.
CPU attach rates in next-generation rack designs.

An order-book air pocket: when duplicate and speculative data-center orders cancel, book-to-bill flips below 1 while newly added industry capacity finally lands — margin mean-reversion follows; the same supply discipline that protects pricing today would then amplify the downturn.
Book-to-bill slipping below 1; first cancellation / reservation-lapse disclosures.

The self-correcting bottleneck cuts both ways: fast Asian supply response commoditises the niche; a technology shift (immersion vs cold plate) can strand lines; sponsor DL written on peak EBITDA multiples carries the reversion risk.
Pricing on new rack-scale awards; entry of large diversified suppliers.

Thin margins are squeezed when memory / GPU costs spike faster than BOM pass-through; platform transitions strand inventory — and that inventory is precisely the ABF collateral; customer concentration mirrors the neocloud problem one step upstream.
Inventory days versus platform launch timing (GB200 → next generation).
White-box erosion of branded share compounds over time; CPO, if adopted, reshapes the switch value chain and the supplier hierarchy with it.

Labour inflation eats fixed-price contracts; cancelled projects strand mobilisation costs; if developers come under stress, payment terms stretch down the subcontractor chain — the factoring collateral weakens exactly when it is most used.
Skilled-trade wage indices; developer payment terms stretching.

Stranded-generation risk: demand fails to arrive after turbine deposits and PPAs are committed; regulatory pushback on co-located deals and grid cost allocation can rewrite economics mid-project; merchant tails carry gas-price exposure.
PPA renegotiation requests; state utility-commission rulings on co-location.

Metro-level oversupply post-2028 brings vacancy and re-leasing at lower rents — residual value is location + power access, and both can be replicated by new supply; tenant credit deterioration (neocloud-tenanted projects) and lease–debt tenor mismatch surface at refi walls.
Pre-leasing rates on new starts; cap-rate direction; tenant-mix disclosures.

Capex cuts are the single variable the whole chain is levered to; AI monetisation lagging a surging depreciation charge pressures FCF (Oracle's cash flow turning negative (press reports, 2026) is the early case); accounting and rating scrutiny of off-balance-sheet SPVs could reprice the structure premium.
Capex guidance revisions; depreciation-to-revenue trajectory; CDS on levered names.

Anchor-contract loss or renegotiation is the existential risk given extreme counterparty concentration; GPU residuals can fall faster than amortisation on a technology transition — the collateral decays with the tech cycle; debt matures years before contracts and assets, so a refi wall meeting wider spreads is the classic failure mode; hyperscalers cut external capacity first once their own builds land.
Backlog-to-revenue conversion; rental-rate rollovers; HY spread direction into 2027–28 maturities.

The funding window can close before breakeven — burn still exceeds revenue; model commoditisation (open-source pressure) compresses pricing; stress surfaces first not at the lab but in its compute vehicles' debt, where the leverage actually sits.
Private-round pricing and secondary discounts; vehicle-level covenant news.

Customers' margins squeezed by token costs feed back into NRR decay — the new diligence item this cycle; AI-native challengers can displace incumbent tools faster than prior transitions; seat-based pricing erodes structurally if AI reduces customer headcount.
Portfolio NRR trends; token-cost share of customer COGS.
Retention is untested through a downturn; model vendors move downstream and absorb application functionality with each release; CAC inflates as the space crowds — growth bought, not earned.
Cohort retention disclosures; feature overlap with each major model release.

Fund Evaluation
The investable fund universe: three types

blocks.html: Type A — pure data center / AI-infrastructure thematic equity. Scarce. The archetype is the AI Infrastructure Partnership (AIP): a US$30bn-target vehicle with a US$7.5bn (25%) sponsor commitment, ~75–80% of the portfolio in data centers plus enabling power, targeting 14–16% gross / 11–13% net IRR with 4–6% cash yield on NAV, and Aligned Data Centers as the first platform investment (AIP pitchbook, Jul-26). Returns are a leveraged expression of the colo landlord economics in Exhibit 11 — development spread plus contracted rent — and the fund inherits the sector cycle in full.

blocks.html: Type B — diversified infrastructure and real-asset funds where data centers are one exposure among several. This is where most exposure actually arrives, in two main variants. The infrastructure variant: Partners Group Next Generation Infrastructure, an evergreen SICAV targeting 10–12% net p.a., running a three-pillar strategy (thematic investing / infrastructure characteristics / asset transformation) across >150 infrastructure positions with a 10–50% secondaries sleeve — its data center look-through is a handful of seed positions (a US hyperscale data center platform at ~2.2% of the portfolio, a distributed-generation provider serving data center clients at ~4.3%, data center site commercialisation, Australian sustainable data centers) (PG NGI PW pitchbook, May-26). The real-estate net-lease variant: Blue Owl Real Estate Fund VI (OREF VI), a triple-net-lease fund whose data center exposure runs through stabilised leases and preferred equity — the book already holds data center leases to CoreWeave (9.7% cap rate, A-), a Meta SPV (11.0%), Oracle (7.8%) and Alphabet (7.0%, AA+), with a further ~US$2.3bn of data center preferred equity and leases under contract at 7.5–8.0% effective cap rates (OREF VI 2Q26 letter, Jun-26). The two variants share the evaluation logic — look-through: how much of NAV and pipeline rests on data center demand, and through which link of the chain — but run different engines: infrastructure development and secondaries versus stabilised landlord income. OREF VI is incidentally live evidence for this report’s tenant-credit-tiering thesis: the same asset class prices from 7.0% (AA+) to 11.0% (SPV) by tenant.

blocks.html: The three types fail differently. A fails on sector beta — the 2028 supply flip, exit cap rates, tenant credit. B fails on the specific positions that leaned on data center demand — stranded generation, renegotiated PPAs, one bad tenant — while the headline strategy still looks intact, which is why look-through matters more than the fund label. C fails like growth equity — portfolio-company execution and exit windows. One distinction cuts across all three: whether cash yield is produced by contracted rent and PPAs (landlord economics — A, and the net-lease variant of B) or manufactured by structuring (revenue-share amortisation, preferred coupons — C, and parts of B). The second can be real, but it is self-liquidating return of capital unless coverage is demonstrated — test the waterfall, not the target.

Five questions, anchored to this report

items: ① Where on the chain does the fund actually sit? Map holdings and pipeline — not the marketing narrative — to the sub-sectors of Exhibit 2. A “digital infrastructure” label can mean colo landlord, power developer, fiber, or neocloud-adjacent growth; each carries a different row of Exhibit 8 and a different risk row in Exhibit 12.

② What does the equity actually earn? Place the strategy on Exhibit 6: top-right equity earns development spreads and contracted rent (infrastructure-style, distributing); bottom-left earns growth and multiple expansion (venture-style, non-distributing). Funds mixing the two should be able to attribute target returns between yield-on-cost uplift, contracted cash flow and exit multiple — if they cannot, the target is a blend of incompatible engines.

③ Bottleneck position: owner or hostage? Against Exhibits 4–5: does the pipeline own the scarce inputs (powered land, interconnection rights, locked turbine and transformer slots, pre-leases) or depend on others delivering them? With construction delay now the base case, a fund whose business plans assume on-time delivery is underwriting the tail as the mean.

④ Where does the cash yield come from? Benchmark stated cash yields against Exhibit 7 anchors (stabilised colo ABS at 4.3%; AIP's own 4–6% target is consistent with landlord economics). A yield well above the collateral's natural level is being manufactured — by structuring, by leverage, or by returning capital — and the distribution waterfall, recycling provisions and coverage ratios will show which.

⑤ Which downside rows apply? Assign each fund its rows from Exhibit 12 and adopt the matching watch items as the monitoring sheet. Two apply to almost every fund in this universe: the 2028 supply flip and counterparty concentration — the same handful of hyperscaler and NVIDIA decisions sit behind most funds' demand assumptions, so cross-fund diversification is smaller than it appears.

blocks.text: Type-specific diligence emphases

items: Type A — pure thematic (AIP). Vintage concentration: a US$30bn fund deploying into 2027–28 completions is a single-vintage bet on the supply flip’s timing. Tenant credit mix and pre-leasing on the development pipeline; exit cap-rate assumptions versus today’s compressed levels; sponsor conflicts where strategic partners are simultaneously investors, suppliers and tenants; fees on committed versus invested capital during a long deployment runway.

Type B — diversified infra / net-lease (PG NGI, OREF VI). Look-through share of NAV and pipeline resting on data center demand, position by position. For evergreen structures: liquidity terms versus the illiquidity of the assets, NAV-based entry pricing, and how secondaries discounts are marked. For power projects: PPA counterparty, tenor and renegotiation triggers; stranded-generation risk where deposits precede signed demand. For net-lease books: tenant credit tiering (the 7.0–11.0% cap-rate spread is the market pricing it), lease–debt tenor matching, and whether preferred equity positions are income or deferred development risk.

Type C — thematic growth around the chain (Digital Alpha). What the cash yield legally is (coupon, revenue share, return of capital) and whether coverage is demonstrated; sourcing concentration — a single corporate partner behind ~50% of deal flow is an origination risk as well as an edge; whether “unleveraged” holds at the structure level, not just the deal level; and which chain counterparties (neoclouds, enterprises) stand behind portfolio-company revenue.
